ut_sunny_side.blurb: Sunny Side is the southeast-facing half of Black Rocks, a small cluster of short, dark basalt walls on the edge of St. George. The routes are quick single pitches of roughly 30 to 40 feet, mostly sport with a good number of trad lines and a few top-ropes. Most of the climbing sits in the 5.8 to 5.10 range, with a handful of harder lines in the low 5.11s. The rock is slick and low in friction, with sharp-edged pockets, so footwork and finger toughness matter. Because it takes the sun, this side is a favorite on cold, clear winter days and gets very hot once the weather warms up.
ut_sunny_side.parking_note: Pull off on the west side of Bluff Street (SR-18) a couple of miles north of town, just beyond the mile 5 marker. The pullout is unmarked and only a short trail walk from the rock.
ut_sunny_side.approach: A short trail leads from the pullout through a fence into the canyon. Drop into the gully, and Sunny Side is the wall on your right as you descend.

ut_monkey_boy_area.blurb: Monkey Boy is a dense cluster of sandstone boulders near the north end of Moe's Valley, one of southern Utah's best-known winter bouldering venues. The problems cover a wide spread, from easy V1s up into the V10 to V12 range, with the bulk falling between about V3 and V9. Moe's Valley is popular for the warm desert stone it offers when snow has buried other areas. The sandstone is fragile when damp, so give it a day or two to dry after rain or snow. Expect crowds on good winter weekends, and bring plenty of pads for the landings.
ut_monkey_boy_area.parking_note: Follow the road to the dedicated Moe's Valley climbing parking, west of the St. George airport. Higher clearance helps on the dirt stretch; low cars can stop where the pavement ends and walk the rest.
ut_monkey_boy_area.approach: From the end of the road, follow the main trail north, passing a distinctive boulder along the way, until you reach the large group of boulders.

ut_mile_385_area.blurb: Mile 385 is a roadside crag in Logan Canyon, named for an old mile marker that has since been renumbered. It is mostly single-pitch sport climbing, with a few trad and top-rope lines and several boulder problems. Routes cluster in the 5.11 and 5.12 range and run up into the low 5.13s, with a small number of easier options. The walk from the road is short, which makes it a handy warm-up or a second stop on a day at the steeper walls nearby. Logan Canyon runs cooler than the rest of northern Utah and snow tends to hang around longer, so the season starts later than on the Wasatch Front.

ut_fin_wall.blurb: Fin Wall is a long sandstone peninsula in Indian Creek, the Wingate sandstone crack-climbing mecca near Bears Ears. All of the climbing here is trad, mostly splitter cracks and finger-to-hand-size lines. The right side offers long, clean walls, while the left side is more broken, with pillars and corners. Grades center on 5.10 and 5.11, with a few steps up into 5.12 and 5.13. The wall sees sun for much of the day through the main season and falls into shade in the afternoon. Expect to carry plenty of cams, since the cracks are sustained and uniform.

ut_china_cave.blurb: China Cave is a big, steep, cave-shaped wall in Logan Canyon, home to some of the hardest sport climbing in Utah. The routes are bolted, overhanging and often linked, and nearly everything falls between 5.12 and 5.14. The bulk sits at 5.13, so it suits climbers who are comfortable on steep, powerful ground. A short trail leads up the canyon from the road to the base of the cave. Snow lingers longer in Logan Canyon than elsewhere in northern Utah, so the season runs later into spring than at crags on the Wasatch Front.

ut_hard_rock.blurb: Hard Rock is one of American Fork Canyon's most popular sport crags, a west-facing limestone wall tucked in the trees near the road. It has a rare spread of grades for the canyon, from a couple of easy 5.6 and 5.7 routes up to 5.13, with the largest group in the 5.10s and a good number of 5.11 and 5.12 lines. The wall is shaded in the morning and picks up strong afternoon sun, so it can be comfortable in both cooler and warmer weather. Limestone in this canyon can be sharp and a little crumbly, and a stick clip is handy on some of the harder routes.
ut_hard_rock.parking_note: Use the Little Mill picnic area on SR-92, on the north side of the road near mile marker 12. It has only a few spaces, so arrive early on busy days.

ut_main_canyon_road_ice.blurb: Main Canyon Road collects the ice that forms along the south wall beside the road through Maple Canyon, a winter alternative to the area's summer cobble sport climbing. The flows are short and approachable, running mostly from WI3 to WI5, with the easiest grade being the most common. A few mixed lines also share the wall. Ice quality swings with the winter, from thin streaks to fat columns, and some flows hide in gullies that are not visible from the road. Plan to be self-sufficient on rappel anchors and keep an eye on the weather, since snow often covers the road in winter.
